turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hello Doctor. I, um... I came in because, well, it’s about church. I’ve been going to the same church for, oh, must be nearly fifty years now, and I always help out with the Sunday potlucks down in the fellowship hall. I love doing it, setting everything up, making sure everyone gets a good hot plate of food. But lately, I just... I keep doing these odd things, and it’s getting folks to staring at me. 

Like just this past week, I was standing by the potluck table, right by the macaroni salad, and I picked up the serving spoon—the big heavy metal one, you know?—and I just held it up in the air. I just stood there holding it up and not moving a single inch. I don't know why, I just froze like a statue with my arm up in the air. 

And then, well, another time, I was in charge of the silverware and the napkins. They buy those nice thick paper napkins, and instead of just setting them out on the table like a normal person, I stood there folding the exact same stack of napkins over and over again. Just smoothing them down, creasing them, folding them, unfolding them, and folding them again. And there was a whole line of people just standing there, waiting on me to just hand them a napkin so they could go sit down and eat their pie, and I just kept folding that same pile. 

I just get stuck doing these strange things, Doctor, and I don't understand it. It’s terribly embarrassing, I mean, I’ve always been the one running the kitchen, I know how to serve a meal, but I just... I don't know what's happening to me. It's got me so upset I almost didn't want to show my face there this Sunday.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes freezing like a statue while holding a spoon (posturing/catalepsy) and repetitively folding the same stack of napkins over and over (stereotypy), which are clear examples of disorganized or abnormal motor behavior.

turns.doctor_question: When you were holding the serving spoon up in the air and folding those napkins over and over, did it feel like something you had to do, like an urge or a compulsion you couldn't resist? Or did it feel more like your body was just stuck or frozen in that position without you consciously deciding to keep doing it?
turns.patient_response:
Well, like I was just saying about that big metal spoon and those napkins, it wasn't like I had an urge to do it. It wasn't like a sudden craving where I thought, oh, I just have to hold this spoon up. Lord, no. It was more like... well, it was exactly like you said, like my body just got stuck. 

With the spoon, my arm just went up to scoop the macaroni salad—Martha makes it with the little diced red peppers, you know, just like her mother used to do before she passed—and my arm went up, and it just... stayed. It was like the motor just cut out right in the middle of the job. I didn't decide to keep it up there. My body just froze up solid as a block of ice. And my mind, well, I was in there thinking, 'Put the spoon down, folks are waiting,' but my arm just wouldn't get the message. It was just stuck there in the air, heavy as lead.

And then with those napkins... oh, my goodness, it wasn't that I felt I needed them to be perfect or anything like that. It was more like my hands just got caught on a loop, like a broken record playing the same skip over and over. I was just folding, and folding, and smoothing that same paper napkin—they buy them in bulk from the warehouse store now, not the nice soft ones we used to have back in the nineties, so they're rough on the hands—and my fingers were just doing it all on their own. I didn't decide to keep doing it. I just couldn't seem to make them stop and do the next thing, which was handing it to Mr. Henderson who was standing right there with his slice of cherry pie just looking at me like I'd lost my marbles. 

So it's just like I told you, I keep doing these odd things at the potluck, just freezing up or repeating the same motion while folks are waiting on me, and it's not me deciding to do it at all. My body just gets entirely stuck.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes their body freezing up like a block of ice and their hands getting caught in a repetitive loop without conscious control, indicating catatonic or stereotypic behavior.
symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient explicitly denies feeling a need for the napkins to be perfect, ruling out symmetry or exactness obsessions.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly denies having an urge or craving to perform the repetitive actions, ruling out compulsions.

turns.doctor_question: When your arm was frozen holding the spoon up in the air, or when your hands were stuck folding those napkins, if someone had tapped you on the shoulder and said 'Stop, put it down right now,' do you think you could have forced yourself to stop and put the spoon down or put the napkins aside? Or would your body just not obey no matter how hard you tried?
turns.patient_response:
Well, that's just the thing of it, Doctor. See, when my arm was up in the air with that spoon—and like I said, it was a heavy one, one of those good sturdy metal ones we've had at the church since Reverend Thomas was there, oh, must be thirty years ago now—I was standing there, frozen stiff. And Mrs. Gable, she was right next to me serving the green beans. She did notice. She leaned over and she touched my arm, right here on the elbow, and she whispered, 'Mary, what on earth are you doing? Serve the macaroni.' 

And you know, I heard her clear as a bell. I wanted to put that spoon down. I was telling my arm, 'Put the spoon down, Mary, put it down right into the bowl.' But... it just wouldn't. It wouldn't obey me at all. No matter how hard I tried to force it, my arm just stayed locked up there in the air until it finally decided to come down on its own sweet time. 

And the same exact thing happened with the napkins. Mr. Henderson, bless his heart, he actually cleared his throat real loud, you know how men do when they're getting impatient, and he said, 'Mary, I just need a napkin for my pie.' He didn't tap my shoulder, but he spoke right to me, loud enough for the whole line to hear. And I tried, Doctor, I really did. I tried to just let go of that paper square and hand it over. But my fingers just kept right on smoothing and folding. It was like my brain was shouting 'stop' and my hands were completely deaf to it. So no, even with folks telling me to stop, I just couldn't make my body mind me. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, just being trapped inside yourself while everybody watches.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes severe disturbances in motor control, including her arm being 'locked up' in the air (catalepsy/posturing) and her fingers continuously folding napkins (stereotypy) despite her conscious efforts to stop.

turns.doctor_question: Mary, when did these freezing episodes and repetitive hand movements first start happening? Was it something that came on suddenly one day, or has it been gradually getting worse over weeks or months?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think on that a minute, Doctor. It certainly didn't just happen overnight, like somebody flipping a light switch, no sir. It's been... oh, I'd say right around six months now. Yes, because it was just about the time we were getting ready for the big Easter sunrise service. We always do a big breakfast after that, with the scrambled eggs and the sausage links. We don't use the patties because the links are just easier to keep warm in those metal chafing dishes they keep down in the church basement, you know, the ones with the little little fire cans underneath them. 

And that's when I first started noticing it, these little spells where my hands would just get stuck doing something odd, like I was telling you with the spoon and the napkins. But it's not just the freezing up, either, Doctor. Folks have been telling me for about that same six months that my talking has gotten all tangled up, too. They say I'm terribly hard to follow, that I just go on and on and they don't know what I'm trying to get at or what I mean. Like my sister-in-law Beatrice, she told me just the other day that she can't make heads or tails of what I'm saying half the time lately. And I don't mean to be confusing, I really don't, I just have so much on my mind and it all comes out at once, but apparently my talking has just been a mess since the spring. 

So yes, I'd say it's been a good six months of this odd behavior and my talking being so hard for people to understand. Six whole months of just feeling like I'm not quite steering my own ship, and it just breaks my heart because I've always prided myself on being sharp as a tack when it comes to organizing the church meals, and now I'm just making a spectacle of myself.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient reports that for the past six months, her talking has been 'tangled up,' 'a mess,' and 'terribly hard to follow' for others.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient confirms experiencing 'freezing up' and spells where her hands get stuck doing odd, repetitive movements.

turns.doctor_question: Mary, besides the trouble with your speech that people have mentioned, have you noticed any changes in your memory, or do you find yourself having trouble with things like remembering names, dates, or keeping track of what you need to do during the day?
turns.patient_response:
Well, memory... yes, I suppose it is my memory, too. It's not just the names, though goodness knows I've known some of these folks since we were in pigtails and suddenly I look at them and just draw a complete blank. But mostly it's the plans, Doctor, keeping track of what I'm supposed to be doing during the week. It's gotten so bad that I've actually had to step back from my choir duties and a lot of my church volunteering. 

I used to handle the schedule for the choir robes, you see, making sure they got picked up and dropped off at the dry cleaners over on Elm Street—the one run by the Miller family, because they give the church a nice discount and they don't use that terrible heavy starch that makes the collars scratch your neck all through the sermon—but lately, I've just been getting all the plans completely mixed up. I'd forget which Sunday we needed the gold sashes and which was the purple, or I'd mix up the dates for the committee meetings and tell people the wrong time to show up, or I'd completely forget who was supposed to bring the communion bread. 

And it just... well, it makes folks uncomfortable. You can see it in their faces. They don't want to say anything harsh, bless their hearts, but I can tell they get real uneasy when I start getting the plans backwards or I show up on the wrong day entirely. And then poor Mrs. Higgins or somebody else has to come in right behind me and completely redo what I was supposed to handle in the first place. They have to make all the phone calls again and fix my messes just to make sure Sunday service goes off right. 

So I just told Pastor Davis that I need to take a step back from the choir and the organizing for a while. It just hurts my pride, Doctor, it really does, having to give up my duties and watch other people redo my work just because I can't keep a simple plan straight in my head anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes frequently forgetting dates, times, and specific tasks related to her volunteer activities.

turns.doctor_question: Mary, have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs, or do your muscles feel tight and stiff? And have you or anyone else noticed any twitching or rippling movements under your skin, especially in your arms, legs, or tongue?
turns.patient_response:
Well, weakness? No, Doctor, I can't say I've felt any weakness at all. My arms are still as strong as they ever were, praise the Lord. Just yesterday I was carrying in the groceries—two heavy paper sacks, mind you, because I don't like those flimsy plastic ones they use nowadays, they always tear right at the bottom the second you put canned goods in them, and I had three heavy cans of sliced peaches and a big tin of Maxwell House coffee in there—and I carried them right up the front steps without a lick of trouble. So my arms are just fine. And my legs, too. I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway every single morning, rain or shine, and that's a good fifty yards down a gravel path, and my legs carry me just fine. 

And as for them feeling tight or stiff... well, no, not really. I mean, my knees might pop a little bit when I first get up out of my good armchair, the floral one in the living room that Arthur bought me for our anniversary years ago, but my muscles themselves aren't stiff or tight like you're asking. Now, when I freeze up like a statue, like I was telling you about with the spoon, well sure, I'm stuck then, but when I'm just going about my normal day and my body is listening to me, my muscles feel perfectly normal. 

And twitching? Rippling under the skin? Oh, goodness gracious, no! That sounds just awful, Doctor, like something out of one of those scary moving pictures my grandson likes to watch on the television, with bugs or something moving around inside a person. No, no, I haven't seen anything like that, and nobody else at the church or in my family has said a word about it either. My skin is just regular old lady skin, a bit thinner and more wrinkled than it used to be, maybe, but nothing is twitching or rippling underneath it, I can promise you that. 

And my tongue? No, no twitching there either. I know I told you my talking gets all tangled up and confusing for folks lately, but my tongue itself works just fine. It's not jumping around in my mouth or anything strange like that. I can still eat my peppermint hard candies and sip my hot tea without biting it or having it spasm on me. So no, Doctor, none of that twitching or weakness, none at all. It's just the freezing up and my mind getting all my plans mixed up that are giving me all this grief.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes episodes where she will 'freeze up like a statue' and get 'stuck,' which is indicative of catatonic behavior such as catalepsy or stupor.

Well, now, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I understand folks perfectly fine. It's like they're searching for the answer about the blankets in all that chatter, and it's just gotten buried. So, no, I don't have trouble understanding them, and I know the words I want to use, but they just tumble out in this big, long river that doesn't go where it's supposed to.

Dr. Henderson down at the vision center on Elm Street—he’s such a polite young man, he took over the whole practice when his father retired and moved down to Boca Raton—he always tells me my eyes are doing remarkably well for a lady of my age. Just yesterday morning, I was looking straight up at the ceiling in the front parlor because I thought I saw a little brown water spot forming right near the crown molding. I am making a lovely little cross-stitch blanket for my great-niece—she is expecting her first baby in August, a little girl, and we are just so thrilled about it—and you have to look down very, very carefully to count all those tiny little stitches on the fabric so you don't mess up the pattern.
